ABSTRACT: Optically active compounds are abundant in nature
and are of fundamental interest for organic, medicinal, and material
chemistry. Catalytic transformation of readily available racemic
compounds into the same value-added enantiomeric products is
one of the most efficient and cost-effective protocols. Herein, an
S
N
2′-type enantioselective reaction of racemic propargylic alcohols
with aryl boronic acids (both are readily available) under a
rhodium catalyst empowered by a new phosphoramidite−olefin
bidentate ligand affording tetrasubstituted enantioenriched allenes has been unveiled. A pair of diastereomeric vinylic rhodium
species with an allylic hydroxyl group has been identified and characterized by ESI-MS and TWIM-MS. Based on the X-ray
diffraction data of the catalyst and other mechanistic studies, it is confirmed that the reaction is a conceptually new approach of
parallel path enantio-convergent transformation, which is different from the classic dynamic kinetic resolution and dynamic kinetic
asymmetric transformations.
■
INTRODUCTION
Optically active stereoisomers often elicit divergent biological
responses owing to the intrinsic discriminatory capacity of
biological systems, which in turn drives a perpetual demand for
highly enantioselective synthetic methodologies toward the
preferred stereoisomers.
1−3
During the last two decades,
optically active compounds bearing central chirality or biaryl
axial chirality have been extensively investigated due to their
profound significance in biologically active natural and artificial
products, chiral ligands, organocatalysts, and multifunctional
synthetic building blocks.
4
As a sharp contrast, allenes exhibit a
distinctly different type of axial chirality that extends across
three contiguous carbons. Given the inherent steric distance
between their 1,3-terminal substituents, the creation of this
type of axial chirality is much more challenging and thus
remains less developed.
Previously, optically active tetrasubstituted allenes
5
have
been originally prepared by applying delicate precursors such
as (di)enynones,
6
allenyl anion equivalents,
7
and 1,3-enynes.
8
Propargylic alcohols and derivatives are readily available and
have been extensively applied as the versatile starting materials
in highly efficient and selective syntheses.
9
In a seminal study,
Jacobsen and co-workers developed the enantioselective
allylation of tertiary propargyl acetates using chiral squaramide
catalysts and TMSOTf as a promoter to construct all-carbon
quaternary chiral centers via a catalytic enantioselective S
N
1
process (Scheme 1a).
10
As a comparison, the free hydroxyl
group in propargylic alcohols is a rather poor leaving group.
The S
N
2′-type substitution reactions of tertiary propargylic
alcohols with a nucleophile would generate the optically active
tetrasubstituted allene.
In 2017, we developed the transition metal-catalyzed syn-β−
OH elimination reaction, which led to the (S)-tetrasubstituted
chiral allenes from (S)-propargylic alcohols and N-methox-
ybenzamide.
11
Very recently, we reported a stereospecific Rh-
catalyzed reaction of (R)-tertiary propargylic alcohols with
organoboronic acids followed by the specific anti- or syn-β-
hydroxyl elimination to afford (S)- or (R)-allenes by applying
[Rh(COD)OH]
2
or Cp*Rh(OAc)
2
as the catalyst, respectively
(Scheme 1b).
12
The Pd-catalyzed kinetic resolution protocol
for the asymmetric carboxylation of tertiary propargylic
alcohols by using PPh
3
as the supporting ligand has also
been developed for the construction of chiral tetrasubstituted
2,3-allenoic acids with the more slowly reacting isomer being
recovered (Scheme 1c).
13
These transformations proceeded
via the concept of either chirality transfer or kinetic resolution,
whereas enantio-convergent synthesis from racemic tertiary
propargylic alcohols remains a significant challenge and has not
been established. Herein, we wish to report S
N
2′-type reactions
of racemic propargylic alcohols with another type of readily
available and easy-to-handle stable chemicals, aryl boronic

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Ligand Development
In order to have an enantio-convergent reaction taking the
controlled syn- and anti-Rh−OH elimination observed in our
previous study,
12
we started our study on the reaction of
racemic 2-phenyloct-3-yn-2-ol rac-1a with 2 equiv of phenyl-
boronic acid 2a with 2.5 mol % [Rh(COD)OH]
2
and a chiral
ligand as a catalyst by running the reaction in THF at 50 °C
(Scheme 2a). Among the typical commercially available chiral
biphosphine ligands (see Scheme S1 in Supporting Informa-
tion for more detailed ligand screening), (R)-BINAP (L1),
16
(S)-SEGphos (L2),
17
(R)-Ph-Garphos (L3),
18
and (R,S)-
Josiphos (L4)
19
afforded the product 3aa in less than 10%
yields with very poor ers. P,N-ligand (R,R)-
i
Pr-Phosferrox
(L5)
20
also did not work well. When (S,S,S)-Ph-SKP (L6),
21
(R)-Ph-SDP (L7),
22
or (R,R)-DIOP (L8)
23
was employed, the
product 3aa was obtained in an essentially racemic form; all
these data indicate a similar level of energy for different
pathways leading to both (R) and (S) enantiomers with similar
efficiency. Both the (R,R)-DACH-Ph Trost ligand (L9)
24
and
(R,R)-Ph-BPE (L10)
25
demonstrated no catalytic activity with
100% recovery of rac-1a. Further investigation on mono-
phosphine ligands indicated the phosphoramidite ligand (R)-
MonoPhos ((R)-L11)
26
could furnish the corresponding
product 3aa in 34% yield with 55:45 er. By switching the
N,N-dimethyl moiety to 2-Me-THQ, i.e., (R)-L12,
27
the
reaction afforded a 31% yield of racemic 3aa. Employment
of N-allyl phosphoramidite ligands (R)-L13 and (S)-L14
28
provided better yields of 73% and 38%, respectively, but the er
was still very low (54:46 er). To our delight, a 27% yield of 3aa
with a much improved er (71:29) was obtained when the
phosphoramidite−olefin ligand (S)-L15
29
was used.
Considering the nature of low yield, we next increased the
loading of the Rh catalyst to 10 mol % to further explore the
chiral Rh catalyst effect as well as solvent and temperature with
the promising ligand (S)-L15 (Table 1). The yield of (R)-3aa
was improved to 87% with 62:38 er when 10 mol %
[Rh(COD)OH]
2
and 12 mol % (S)-L15 were employed
(Table 1, entry 1). Interestingly, the acetylacetonyl Rh
catalysts, Rh(acac)(COE)
2
, could furnish the desired allene
(R)-3aa in 81% yield with 65:35 er (Table 1, entry 2; see Table
S1 in Supporting Information for the detailed screening of the
Rh catalyst), a promising result possibly following the concept
of PPET. Reducing the catalyst loading to 5 mol % resulted in
a decrease in the yield to 58%, while the er value of (R)-3aa
was comparable (Table 1, entry 3). Then, we adjusted the
molar ratio of phenylboronic acid 2a over propargylic alcohol
rac-1a to 1:2, and the er of (R)-3aa could be further improved
to 78:22 (Table 1, entry 4), which indicated that the reactant
stoichiometry was responsible for the improvement of the
enantioselectivity. The temperature effect revealed the reaction
at a lower temperature of 40 °C unexpectedly resulted in a
diminished yield and er, while the reaction at a higher
temperature (60 °C) effectively afforded the product (R)-3aa
in 70% yield with 79:21 er (Table 1, entries 5 and 6). This is
due to the higher reaction temperature, which accelerated the
conversion of (S)-1a to (R)-3aa (for details, see Supporting
Information). The solvent effect was subsequently evaluated:
the reactions in dioxane gave (R)-3aa in 72% yield with 87:13
er (Table 1, entry 7; see Table S1 in the Supporting
Information for the detailed screening of solvents). The
reaction at a lower reaction concentration of 0.1 M contributed
to better enantioselectivity, providing (R)-3aa in 64% yield
with 91:9 er (Table 1, entries 8 and 9).
Encouraged by these data, we further optimized the
backbone of the ligand for the purpose of improving the
enantioselectivity (Scheme 2b). Besides binol-derived skeleton
(S)-L15, semihydrogenated binol-derived skeleton (S)-L16,
vanol-derived skeleton (R)-L17, and spinol-derived skeleton
(R)-L18 all failed to improve the enantioselectivity. Then, we
explored the influence of different substituents at the 6,6′- or
3,3′-position of the binaphthyl skeleton: neither yield nor er
was improved when 6,6′-dibromo- ((S)-L19) or 6,6′-diphenyl
((S)-L20) was applied. With 3,3′-dimethyl-substituted (S)-
L21, the product (R)-3aa was obtained in 69% yield with an
87:13 er; no better results were observed when 3,3′-dibromo-
or 3,3′- diphenyl-substituted ligands (S)-L22 and (S)-L23
were tested. To our delight, an 86% yield of (R)-3aa with 93:7
er was obtained upon applying the TMS substituent at the
3,3′-position of the binaphthyl skeleton ((S)-L24). Increasing
propargylic alcohol rac-1a to 2.1 equiv afforded (R)-3aa in
79% yield with 95:5 er. Importantly, only trace amounts of the
products were formed when the C�C bond hydrogenated
analogue phosphoramidite ligand (S)-L25 was employed,
indicating a critical role of this C�C bond in the 7-membered
ring of (S)-L24.

reaction, we tried to synthesize complex Rh(S)-L24(acac) by
mixing Rh(COE)

with Ag(acac), Rh(S)-L24(acac) was successfully
isolated and characterized by X-ray single-crystal diffraction
study, further confirming that both the P atom and the C�C
bond are coordinated to the Rh atom (Figure 1b). Indeed, the
reaction with Rh((S)-L24)(acac) as a catalyst afforded (R)-3aa
in 74% NMR yield with 94:6 er (Figure 1c, entry 3), which was
similar to the data observed under the standard conditions
(Figure 1c, entry 4), confirming that it is the catalytically active
chiral catalyst for this reaction. Further control experiments
showed that the reaction of propargyl methyl ether under the
standard conditions afforded (R)-3aa in 82% yield with,
however, an enantiomeric ratio of 59:41, indicating the
importance of this hydroxy group in propargylic alcohol
(Figure 1d, eq 1). The reaction of secondary propargylic
alcohol rac-1a″ under the standard conditions afforded
trisubstituted allenes 3aa″ in 2% yield with 35% recovery
(Figure 1d, eq 2), indicating the importance of the tertiary
alcohol unit.
The Mechanistic Studies
In order to investigate the reaction mechanism, the reaction
progress of racemic and chiral propargylic alcohol (R)-1a or
(S)-1a had been monitored (Figure 2). Under the standard
conditions, the reaction of rac-1a afforded the product (R)-3aa
with high ee. The ee of recovered 1a was only 22% with the
(R)-isomer in excess at the time the reaction was complete
(Figure 2a), which excluded the classic kinetic resolution
process. The reaction was complete after 3.5 h; thus, the ee for
1a levels off after that. When (S)-1a was applied (Figure 2b),
the product (R)-3aa was obtained with >90% ee, and the ee of
recovered (S)-1a remained unchanged (>99%) throughout the
reaction. When (R)-1a was applied (Figure 2c), the reaction
also yielded (R)-3aa as the major product, and the ee of
recovered (R)-1a remained unchanged (>99%). All these data
excluded the dynamic kinetic resolution process. Only the E-
isomer of 4aa was formed exclusively from either (S)-1a or
(R)-1a, indicating no isomerization occurred to the in situ
formed allylic C�C bond (Figure 2b,c), which excluded a
DyKAT process via the possible E to Z isomerization of the
C�C bond in the vinyl-rhodium intermediates formed from
the insertion of the C−C triple bond of propargylic alcohol
into the aryl−rhodium bond (for more information, see
Supporting Information Figure S28). By comparison of Figure
2b with Figure 2c, a higher yield was observed in the reaction
profile of (S)-1a. The conversion of (S)-1a was a lower barrier
than that of (R)-1a, leaving a greater amount of (R)-1a
unreacted, which resulted in an increase in its ee value (Figure
2a). A nearly linear effect was observed at both lower (∼10%)
and higher conversions (∼80%), which suggested that the
monomeric complex of Rh with (S)-L24 may be the active
catalytic species. It is consistent with our mechanistic studies
that Rh(S)-L24(acac) is the active species for this trans-
formation (Figure 1c).
30
Based on these results, a unique mechanism has been
proposed in Figure 2e. The syn-insertion of the C−C triple
bond into the Ph-RhL24 species would lead to a pair of
diastereoisomeric vinylic metallic species Int A and Int B (a
pair of diastereoisomers), respectively, which would form the
side product allylic alcohol (R)- or (S)-4aa upon proto-
demetalation.
31
Their subsequent anti- or syn-β−OH elimi-
nation for Int A or Int B in the same chemical environment,
respectively, led to the same chiral allene (R)-3aa.
Now the challenge is to detect the key intermediates
involved in the catalytic cycle. For such a purpose, multi-
dimensional mass spectrometry of electrospray ionization mass
spectrometry (ESI-MS)
32
and traveling-wave ion-mobility
mass spectrometry (TWIM-MS)
33
has been employed to
monitor the reaction of rac-1a (Figure 3). Ions with m/z =
1032 were detected (for more information, see Supporting
Information). To obtain more structural information about
these intermediates, TWIM-MS experiments, which are able to
separate ions according to their various sizes and shapes, have
been performed. As shown in Figure 3a,b, the captured
intermediate ions with m/z = 1032 were resolved into two

Based on the results of DFT studies, we propose the
mechanism outlined in Figure 4. Initially, regioselective syn-
insertion of the C−C triple bond of propargylic alcohol (S)-1a
or (R)-1a to the aryl-rhodium species formed from trans-
metalation of the Rh(I) catalyst with arylboronic acid gave the
vinyl-rhodium IntA or IntB, which have been detected,
separated, and characterized by MS studies (Figure 3). With
the assistance of boric acid molecules and water, IntA may
proceed with anti-β−OH elimination via the ten-membered
cyclic transition state (S)-TS2_anti, while its diastereoisomer
IntB generated from (R)-1a takes syn-β−OH elimination via
the ten-membered cyclic transition state (R)-TS2_syn, both
leading to the formation of the same enantiomer, tetrasub-
stituted allene (R)-3aa.
Substrate Scope
Having confirmed the PPET protocol and identified the
optimal conditions, we next explored the generality of this Rh-
catalyzed asymmetric coupling reaction between racemic
tertiary propargylic alcohols and aryl boronic acids (Figure
5). Various commercially available aryl boronic acids were
tested first. The model reaction with phenylboronic acid on a
0.5 mmol scale delivered the tetrasubstituted allene (R)-3aa in
81% yield with 95:5 er. The reaction of 3- or 4-methyl-
substituted phenylboronic acids afforded (R)-3ab or (R)-3ac
in 68% or 74% yield with 95:5 er, while the 2-methyl-
substituted phenylboronic acid gave the product (R)-3ad in
moderate er (78:22) most probably because of the steric effect.
Other electron-donating groups, such as ethyl, tert-butyl, 3,5-
dimethyl, phenyl, and 3-methoxy-substituted phenylboronic
acids, all afforded the products (R)-3ae-3ai in decent yields of
45−71% with decent enantioselectivities (93:7−97:3 ers). 2-
Naphthylboronic acid was also suitable to form the
corresponding product (R)-3aj. The electron-deficient 4-
bromo and 4- methoxycarbonyl-substituted phenylboronic
acids also worked to give (R)-3ak and (R)-3al in 53% yield
with 91:9 er and 50% yield with 92:8 er, respectively.
Moreover, phenylboronic acid containing other synthetically
useful or highly active functional groups including trimethyl-
silyl, vinyl, ethoxycarbonylethenyl, and bromomethyl also
afforded the products (R)-3am-3ap in 44−79% yields with
93:7−96:4 ers.
Then, different tertiary propargylic alcohols with phenyl-
boronic acid were evaluated. Electron-donating groups, such as
methyl, methoxy, and isopropyl, and electron-withdrawing
groups, including fluoro, chloro, bromo, 4-bromophenyl, and
methoxycarbonyl, were well accommodated within the phenyl
ring substituent of R

could be easily removed with camphorsulfonic acid to afford

enantiopurity; moreover, (S)-3ua could readily react with
phthalimide or NBS to give the product N-allenyl phthalimide
(S)-6 or allenyl bromide (S)-7 in excellent yields with a similar

(S)-8 in 80% yield with 94:6 er.
■
CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we herein observed a parallel path enantio-
convergent transformation (PPET) for racemic alcohols: a
rhodium-catalyzed asymmetric coupling reaction between
readily available racemic propargylic alcohols and aryl boronic
